core_concepts.title: Having: у меня есть
core_concepts.lesson: Russian expresses possession as something existing 'by' a person. Learn the whole frame before producing genitive endings.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I have a book.
core_concepts.hint: Use у + person + есть.

core_concepts.title: Not having: у меня нет
core_concepts.lesson: Absence uses the fixed frame у + person + нет. Treat the following form as part of the phrase for now.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I have no time.
core_concepts.hint: Use у + person + нет.

core_concepts.title: Location chunks
core_concepts.lesson: Learn common locations as whole phrases with в/на: в школе, на работе. The ending system comes later.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I am at school.
core_concepts.hint: Where? Use a learned в/на location chunk.

core_concepts.title: Experiencer chunks
core_concepts.lesson: Russian often puts the person experiencing a feeling in forms such as мне/тебе. Learn these high-frequency frames whole.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I like music.
core_concepts.hint: Use мне/тебе + experience.

core_concepts.title: With someone
core_concepts.lesson: Learn с + person as a useful whole phrase. Productive instrumental endings unlock later.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I am going with a friend.
core_concepts.hint: Together with: с + learned form.

core_concepts.title: Noun gender
core_concepts.lesson: Every Russian noun is masculine, feminine, or neuter. You usually can tell from the ending: a consonant or -й is masculine, -а/-я is feminine, -о/-е is neuter. Gender matters because adjectives and past-tense verbs change their endings to match the noun.
core_concepts.exampleEn: table (masculine) · book (feminine) · window (neuter)
core_concepts.hint: Ending → gender: consonant/-й = masculine, -а/-я = feminine, -о/-е = neuter.

core_concepts.title: Making plurals
core_concepts.lesson: To talk about more than one thing, most masculine and feminine nouns add -ы or -и, and most neuter nouns change -о/-е to -а/-я. This is the plural you use as the subject of a sentence.
core_concepts.exampleRu: стол → столы · книга → книги · окно → окна
core_concepts.exampleEn: table → tables · book → books · window → windows
core_concepts.hint: Plural: usually -ы/-и; neuter -о/-е → -а/-я.

core_concepts.title: The accusative (direct object)
core_concepts.lesson: The accusative marks the direct object — the thing the action happens to. Masculine inanimate and neuter nouns look the same as the dictionary form; feminine nouns change -а → -у and -я → -ю.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I'm reading a book. (книга → книгу)
core_concepts.hint: Direct object → accusative. Feminine -а → -у, -я → -ю.

core_concepts.title: The genitive ("of", absence)
core_concepts.lesson: The genitive shows possession or "of" something, and is used for absence (нет + genitive) and after words like без, из, у. Masculine/neuter nouns usually take -а/-я; feminine -а/-я become -ы/-и.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I have no time. (время → времени)
core_concepts.hint: "of" / нет / без / из / у → genitive.

core_concepts.title: The prepositional (location)
core_concepts.lesson: The prepositional only appears after a preposition — mainly в/на for location ("in/at") and о for a topic ("about"). Most nouns simply take the ending -е.
core_concepts.exampleEn: The book is on the table. (стол → столе)
core_concepts.hint: After в/на (where) and о (about) → prepositional, usually -е.

core_concepts.title: The dative ("to/for")
core_concepts.lesson: The dative marks the recipient — the person something is given, said, or shown to. It also appears after к and по, and in age and "need" phrases. Masculine/neuter take -у/-ю; feminine take -е.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I'm writing to a friend. (друг → другу)
core_concepts.hint: Recipient "to/for", к, по, age → dative.

core_concepts.title: The instrumental ("with/by")
core_concepts.lesson: The instrumental shows the means "by/with" which something is done, and follows с ("together with"). Masculine/neuter take -ом/-ем; feminine take -ой/-ей.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I write with a pen. (ручка → ручкой)
core_concepts.hint: Means "by/with", and с (together with) → instrumental.

core_concepts.title: The past tense
core_concepts.lesson: The Russian past tense is easy: drop -ть and add -л for a male subject, -ла for female, -ло for neuter, -ли for plural. It agrees with the subject's gender and number, not the person.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он читал. Она читала. Они читали.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He read. She read. They read.
core_concepts.hint: Past = stem + -л/-ла/-ло/-ли (agrees with subject gender/number).

core_concepts.title: Adjective agreement
core_concepts.lesson: Adjectives copy the gender and number of the noun they describe. The dictionary form is masculine (-ый/-ий); feminine ends -ая, neuter -ое, and plural -ые/-ие.
core_concepts.exampleRu: новый дом · новая книга · новое окно · новые дома
core_concepts.exampleEn: new house · new book · new window · new houses
core_concepts.hint: Adjective matches its noun: -ый/-ий/-ой (masculine), -ая/-яя (feminine), -ое/-ее (neuter), -ые/-ие (plural).

core_concepts.title: The present tense
core_concepts.lesson: Russian present tense uses six personal forms: я, ты, он/она/оно, мы, вы, они. The hard part is the stem: common verbs change consonants or vowels, so learn the full mini-paradigm instead of guessing from the infinitive.
core_concepts.exampleRu: писать -> пишу, пишешь, пишет; любить -> люблю, любишь, любит
core_concepts.exampleEn: to write -> I write, you write, he writes; to love -> I love, you love, he loves
core_concepts.hint: Present: learn the stored stem pattern; watch mutations like писать -> пишу, любить -> люблю.

core_concepts.title: Verb aspect
core_concepts.lesson: Most Russian verbs come in pairs. The imperfective describes an ongoing or repeated action ("was doing"); the perfective describes a single completed action with a result ("did / got done"). Choose by whether the action reached its end.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Я писал письмо. / Я написал письмо.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I was writing a letter. / I wrote (finished) a letter.
core_concepts.hint: Ongoing/repeated = imperfective; completed result = perfective.

core_concepts.title: The future tense
core_concepts.lesson: Russian has two futures. The imperfective future uses бу́ду, бу́дешь, бу́дет … plus the imperfective infinitive (ongoing/repeated). The perfective future is just the perfective verb conjugated like the present — it already means a single completed future action.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Я бу́ду чита́ть. / Я прочита́ю кни́гу.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I will be reading. / I will read (finish) the book.
core_concepts.hint: Future: буду + imperfective inf, OR conjugated perfective.

core_concepts.title: Commands (imperative)
core_concepts.lesson: To tell someone to do something, take the present-tense stem and add -й (after a vowel), -и (after a consonant, stressed), or -ь. Add -те for polite/plural. Imperfective invites; perfective asks for one result.
core_concepts.exampleEn: Read! Read (pl.)! Write the letter.
core_concepts.hint: Command: stem + -й/-и(+те). Perfective = one result.

core_concepts.title: Reflexive verbs (-ся)
core_concepts.lesson: Verbs ending in -ся/-сь turn the action back on the subject or make it intransitive: учи́ть (teach) → учи́ться (study), нача́ть (begin sth) → нача́ться (begin, of itself). The ending is -ся after a consonant, -сь after a vowel.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I study. The lesson begins.
core_concepts.hint: -ся/-сь = action on oneself / intransitive.

core_concepts.title: Comparing things
core_concepts.lesson: For "more", most adjectives and adverbs add -ее (бы́стрый → быстре́е), with some irregulars (хоро́ший → лу́чше, большо́й → бо́льше). "Than" is чем, or put the compared thing in the genitive.
core_concepts.exampleEn: This book is more interesting. Moscow is bigger.
core_concepts.hint: More: adjective + -ее (лучше/больше). "Than" = чем or genitive.

core_concepts.title: Can, must, need (dative)
core_concepts.lesson: "Possible/allowed" мо́жно, "necessary" на́до/ну́жно, "impossible/forbidden" нельзя́ are used with the dative of the person and an infinitive. There is no "to be" in the present.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Мне на́до рабо́тать. Здесь мо́жно кури́ть?
core_concepts.exampleEn: I need to work. May one smoke here?
core_concepts.hint: надо/нужно/можно/нельзя + dative person + infinitive.

core_concepts.title: Verbs of motion (go)
core_concepts.lesson: Russian splits "go" by manner and direction. Use идти́/е́хать for one trip in one direction now; ходи́ть/е́здить for repeated, round, or general movement. идти́/ходи́ть = on foot, е́хать/е́здить = by vehicle.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Я иду́ в шко́лу. Я ча́сто хожу́ в парк.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I'm going to school (now). I often go to the park.
core_concepts.hint: идти/ехать = one trip now; ходить/ездить = repeated/round.

core_concepts.title: One's own (свой)
core_concepts.lesson: свой means "one's own" and refers back to the subject of the clause. It agrees like мой. Use it instead of его/её/их when the owner is the subject, to avoid ambiguity.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He is reading his (own) book.
core_concepts.hint: свой = belonging to the subject; agrees like мой.

core_concepts.title: Prefixed motion verbs
core_concepts.lesson: Prefixes add direction to motion verbs: при- (arrive), у- (leave), в-/во- (enter), вы- (exit), по- (set off). On идти-type stems they form aspect pairs (приходи́ть/прийти́).
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он пришёл домо́й и ушёл сно́ва.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He came home and left again.
core_concepts.hint: при-=arrive, у-=leave, в-=enter, вы-=exit, по-=set off.

core_concepts.title: Would / conditional (бы)
core_concepts.lesson: The particle бы plus a past-tense verb expresses a hypothetical: "would". For "if", use е́сли бы … (past), … бы … (past) in both clauses.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Я бы помо́г. Е́сли бы я знал, я бы сказа́л.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I would help. If I had known, I would have said.
core_concepts.hint: бы + past = "would". Если бы … , … бы …

core_concepts.title: Which / who (который)
core_concepts.lesson: кото́рый links clauses ("which/who/that"). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to, but takes its case from its role in its own clause.
core_concepts.exampleEn: The book that I'm reading is interesting.
core_concepts.hint: который: gender/number from antecedent, case from its own clause.

core_concepts.title: The most (superlative)
core_concepts.lesson: The most common superlative puts са́мый (agreeing like an adjective) before the adjective. Some forms also use -ейший/-айший.
core_concepts.exampleEn: This is the most interesting city.
core_concepts.hint: самый + adjective = "the most".

core_concepts.title: In order to (чтобы)
core_concepts.lesson: что́бы expresses purpose. With the same subject, use чтобы + infinitive. With a different subject, use чтобы + past tense (the subjunctive use).
core_concepts.exampleRu: Я чита́ю, что́бы учи́ться. Я хочу́, что́бы ты пришёл.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I read in order to study. I want you to come.
core_concepts.hint: чтобы + infinitive (same subj) / + past (different subj).

core_concepts.title: Numbers and nouns
core_concepts.lesson: After numbers the noun changes: 1 → nominative; 2–4 → genitive singular; 5 and up → genitive plural. This also follows ско́лько and мно́го.
core_concepts.exampleRu: одна́ кни́га, две кни́ги, пять книг
core_concepts.exampleEn: one book, two books, five books
core_concepts.hint: 1 → nom; 2–4 → gen sg; 5+ → gen pl.

core_concepts.title: Predicate short forms
core_concepts.lesson: Many adjectives have a short form used only as the predicate (after an implied "is/are", never before a noun): drop the full ending and add nothing for masculine, -а for feminine, -о for neuter, -ы/-и for plural. You already know до́лжен this way. Short forms describe a temporary state or judgment; the full form (краси́вый, etc.) still names an inherent quality.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он рад. Она́ ра́да. Мы ра́ды.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He is glad. She is glad. We are glad.
core_concepts.hint: Predicate-only form: masculine (bare stem), feminine -а, neuter -о, plural -ы/-и.

core_concepts.title: Active participles
core_concepts.lesson: Active participles work like "-ing/who-does" adjectives. Present: stem + -ущ/-ющ/-ащ/-ящ + adjective endings; past: -вш-. They agree with their noun and replace a кото́рый clause where that noun is the subject.
core_concepts.exampleEn: the person reading a book (who reads a book)
core_concepts.hint: Active participle = "who does X"; agrees like an adjective.

core_concepts.title: Passive participles
core_concepts.lesson: Passive participles mean "-ed/being done". Present: -ем/-им; past: -нн/-енн/-т. The short past form (-н, -на, -но, -ны) builds the perfect passive: «письмо́ напи́сано»
core_concepts.exampleEn: the book written by him; the letter is written
core_concepts.hint: Passive participle = "X-ed"; short form -н/-на/-но/-ны = result.

core_concepts.title: Verbal adverbs (gerunds)
core_concepts.lesson: A gerund (деепричастие) describes a secondary action by the same subject. Imperfective: stem + -я ("while doing"); perfective: -в/-вши ("having done"). It never changes form.
core_concepts.exampleEn: Reading the letter, he was silent.
core_concepts.hint: Gerund: -я (while doing) / -в (having done); invariable.

core_concepts.title: Passive constructions
core_concepts.lesson: Russian forms the passive two ways: with a reflexive imperfective verb (дом строи́тся — "the house is being built") or with a short passive participle for completed results (дом постро́ен). The agent, if named, goes in the instrumental.
core_concepts.exampleEn: The house is being built by workers. The treaty is signed.
core_concepts.hint: Passive: -ся verb (process) or short participle (result); agent = instrumental.

core_concepts.title: Reported speech
core_concepts.lesson: Russian keeps the original tense in reported speech (no backshift). Use что for statements, ли for yes/no questions, and the original question word otherwise.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он сказа́л, что рабо́тает. Я спроси́л, придёт ли он.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He said (that) he works. I asked whether he would come.
core_concepts.hint: Reported: что / ли / question word; tense doesn't shift.

core_concepts.title: Connecting ideas
core_concepts.lesson: Cohesive C1 writing chains clauses with connectors: одна́ко (however), поэ́тому (therefore), несмотря́ на то что (despite the fact that), в то вре́мя как (whereas), благодаря́ тому́ что (thanks to). They let you subordinate and contrast precisely.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Несмотря́ на то что бы́ло тру́дно, он успе́л.
core_concepts.exampleEn: Despite the fact that it was hard, he made it in time.
core_concepts.hint: однако / поэтому / несмотря на то что / в то время как.

core_concepts.title: Nominal style
core_concepts.lesson: Formal Russian prefers verbal nouns over verbs: реши́ть → приня́тие реше́ния (taking a decision), разви́ть → разви́тие. This dense nominal style dominates official and academic registers.
core_concepts.exampleEn: taking the decision took time
core_concepts.hint: Formal register nominalises verbs: решить → принятие решения.

core_concepts.title: Fine points of aspect
core_concepts.lesson: Beyond completion, aspect carries nuance: the imperfective can deny a fact (Я не чита́л — "I didn't read it"), state a general fact, or soften; the perfective stresses result and single occurrence. Negated commands usually take the imperfective.
core_concepts.exampleEn: Don't read this! / Read this (through)!
core_concepts.hint: Imperfective: process/fact/negated commands; perfective: single result.

core_concepts.title: Register and style
core_concepts.lesson: C1 control means matching register: neutral vs. bookish/official (данный = "this", осуществля́ть = "carry out", в связи́ с = "in connection with") vs. colloquial. Word choice signals formality as much as grammar.
core_concepts.exampleEn: in connection with this decision (formal)
core_concepts.hint: Match register: officialese (данный, осуществлять, в связи с) vs. neutral.

core_concepts.title: Set phrases and idiom
core_concepts.lesson: Fluent Russian relies on fixed collocations and idioms whose meaning isn't literal: име́ть в виду́ (to mean), приня́ть во внима́ние (to take into account), име́ть значе́ние (to matter). Learn them as whole units.
core_concepts.exampleEn: I mean something else.
core_concepts.hint: Learn set phrases whole: иметь в виду, принять во внимание.

core_concepts.title: Hedging and reported stance
core_concepts.lesson: Near-native Russian marks the speaker's distance from a quoted claim with reporting particles: мол and де́скать flag casual reported speech ("so they say"), я́кобы signals the claim may be false ("allegedly"), and вро́де бы softens a statement ("sort of"). None of these change the sentence's grammar — they only signal the speaker's stance toward it.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он сказа́л, мол, всё гото́во, но э́то я́кобы непра́вда.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He said - so he claims - everything's ready, but that's allegedly not true.
core_concepts.hint: мол/дескать = casual reported speech; якобы = doubted claim; вроде бы = soft hedge.

core_concepts.title: Emphasis and contrast particles
core_concepts.lesson: A small set of particles carry pure emphasis with no dictionary translation of their own: ведь appeals to something the listener should already accept ("after all"), всё-та́ки signals a stubborn contrast ("still, despite that"), уж intensifies ("quite, indeed"), and лишь restricts ("only, merely", more literary than то́лько).
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он ведь зна́л об э́том, но всё-та́ки не сказа́л ни сло́ва.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He knew about it, after all, but still didn't say a word.
core_concepts.hint: ведь = appeals to shared knowledge; всё-таки = despite that; уж = indeed; лишь = only.

core_concepts.title: Literary connectors
core_concepts.lesson: Formal and literary Russian has its own tier of subordinators above the C1 set: и́бо ("for", explains a cause), да́бы (archaic "in order that"), поско́льку ("insofar as, since"), and the phrase всле́дствие того́ что ("owing to the fact that") for citing a cause formally.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Он не отве́тил, поско́льку не был уве́рен, и́бо вопро́с был сло́жным.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He didn't answer, since he wasn't sure, for the question was complex.
core_concepts.hint: ибо = for; дабы = in order that (archaic); поскольку = insofar as; вследствие того что = owing to.

core_concepts.title: Emphatic word order
core_concepts.lesson: Russian word order is freer than English, and near-native speakers use that freedom deliberately: fronting a word with и́менно marks it as the precise focus ("this one, specifically"), недаро́м implies the following clause is no coincidence, тем не ме́нее pivots to a contrast, and в свою́ о́чередь hands the topic to the next actor in turn.
core_concepts.exampleRu: И́менно он реши́л вопро́с; она́, в свою́ о́чередь, начала́ но́вый прое́кт.
core_concepts.exampleEn: He specifically was the one who solved it; she, in turn, started a new project.
core_concepts.hint: именно = precisely this one; недаром = no accident; тем не менее = nonetheless; в свою очередь = in turn.

core_concepts.title: Deeper hypotheticals
core_concepts.lesson: Beyond the B1 бы conditional, C2 control includes concessive бы chains: что бы ни / как бы ни + past tense ("no matter what/how"), е́сли бы не ("if not for") for a counterfactual condition, and хотя́ бы ("at least") for a minimal concession.
core_concepts.exampleRu: Что бы ни случи́лось, е́сли бы не твоя́ по́мощь, я бы не спра́вился.
core_concepts.exampleEn: Whatever happened, if not for your help, I wouldn't have managed.
core_concepts.hint: что/как бы ни = no matter what/how; если бы не = if not for; хотя бы = at least.

staged_specs.title: Question formation
staged_specs.lesson: Russian yes/no questions use the same word order as statements — only rising intonation (or a question mark in writing) signals a question, with no auxiliary verb needed. Question words (кто, что, где, когда, почему) go at the front, just like in English.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Ты говоришь по-русски?
staged_specs.exampleEn: Do you speak Russian?
staged_specs.hint: No 'do' — just raise your intonation, or start with a question word.

staged_specs.title: And, but, and contrast: и/а/но
staged_specs.lesson: И adds a parallel fact, а marks a mild contrast or shift between two different subjects, and но marks a stronger, more surprising contrast within the same idea.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я хочу поехать, но у меня нет денег.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I want to go, but I don't have any money.
staged_specs.hint: и = and (add); а = but (shift subject); но = but (contradict).

staged_specs.title: Cardinal numbers 0–100
staged_specs.lesson: Numbers 5 and above take genitive plural nouns, 2–4 take genitive singular, and 1 (and compounds ending in 1) agrees like an adjective — full case rules come later; for now, just learn to count.
staged_specs.exampleRu: У меня три брата и одна сестра.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I have three brothers and one sister.
staged_specs.hint: 1 agrees like an adjective; 2–4 and 5+ change the noun's ending (details later).

staged_specs.title: Telling time
staged_specs.lesson: The hour is named with an ordinal number one ahead of the completed hour, and the half-hour is 'half of the next hour' — половина седьмого is half past six, not half past seven.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Сейчас половина седьмого.
staged_specs.exampleEn: It's half past six.
staged_specs.hint: Half-hour = half OF the next (ordinal) hour.

staged_specs.title: Ordinals and dates
staged_specs.lesson: Dates use an ordinal number in the neuter genitive (agreeing with an implied 'число'), followed by the month in genitive: первое мая (May 1st) becomes первого мая when saying when something happened.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я родился первого мая.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I was born on May 1st.
staged_specs.hint: Date = ordinal (genitive neuter) + month (genitive).

staged_specs.title: Two, three, four + genitive singular
staged_specs.lesson: The numbers 2, 3, and 4 (and any number ending in them, like 22, 23) take a noun in the genitive SINGULAR, not the plural you might expect.
staged_specs.exampleRu: На столе лежат два журнала.
staged_specs.exampleEn: There are two magazines on the table.
staged_specs.hint: 2, 3, 4 (and 22, 23, 24…) + genitive singular noun.

staged_specs.title: Five and above + genitive plural
staged_specs.lesson: Numbers 5 and above (and any number ending in 5-9 or 0) take a noun in the genitive PLURAL — the same case used after 'много'.
staged_specs.exampleRu: В комнате было пять студентов.
staged_specs.exampleEn: There were five students in the room.
staged_specs.hint: 5+ (and …5, …6…9, …0) + genitive plural noun.

staged_specs.title: Aspect in the past
staged_specs.lesson: In the past tense, imperfective describes an ongoing or repeated action (or just states that it happened, with no focus on completion), while perfective marks a single completed action with a clear result.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Вчера я читал книгу, а потом прочитал журнал.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Yesterday I was reading a book, and then I finished a magazine.
staged_specs.hint: Imperfective = ongoing/repeated/fact-of; perfective = completed, one result.

staged_specs.title: Aspect in the future
staged_specs.lesson: Imperfective future is built with быть + infinitive and describes an ongoing or repeated future action; perfective future uses the verb's own conjugated (non-past) form and describes a single completed action.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Завтра я буду читать книгу и прочитаю первую главу.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Tomorrow I will be reading a book, and I will finish the first chapter.
staged_specs.hint: Imperfective future = буду + infinitive; perfective future = conjugated perfective verb.

staged_specs.title: Aspect after modals and phase verbs
staged_specs.lesson: Phase verbs like начать (start) and продолжать (continue) take an imperfective infinitive, since they describe a process being begun or continued, not completed.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я начал учить русский язык.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I started learning Russian.
staged_specs.hint: начать/продолжать/закончить + imperfective infinitive (the process itself).

staged_specs.title: Aspect in commands
staged_specs.lesson: A positive command usually uses the perfective verb for a one-time request with a clear result, while the imperfective is used for general invitations, repeated actions, or when politely softening the request.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Закрой дверь, пожалуйста!
staged_specs.exampleEn: Close the door, please!
staged_specs.hint: One-time result = perfective command; general/repeated/softened = imperfective.

staged_specs.title: Aspect under negation
staged_specs.lesson: Negative commands almost always use the imperfective, even when the positive version would be perfective — не закрывай (don't close, general) rather than не закрой, which would sound like a warning against an accident.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Не закрывай дверь — здесь жарко.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Don't close the door — it's hot in here.
staged_specs.hint: Negative commands normally use imperfective, even where a positive one would be perfective.

staged_specs.title: идти/ехать: motion in one direction
staged_specs.lesson: Идти (on foot) and ехать (by vehicle) describe motion happening in one direction, right now, toward a specific destination — not a habit or round trip.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я иду в магазин.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I'm walking to the store right now.
staged_specs.hint: One trip, one direction, happening now: идти (on foot) / ехать (by vehicle).

staged_specs.title: ходить/ездить: habitual and round-trip motion
staged_specs.lesson: Ходить and ездить describe motion that's habitual, repeated, or a round trip (there and back) — not a single trip in one direction.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я каждый день хожу в школу.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I go to school every day.
staged_specs.hint: Habit, repetition, or round trip: ходить (on foot) / ездить (by vehicle).

staged_specs.title: Carrying and leading motion verbs
staged_specs.lesson: Нести/носить (carrying something by hand) and вести/водить (leading someone, or driving a vehicle) follow the same one-direction-vs-habitual pattern as идти/ходить, just for motion with an object or companion.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Мама ведёт ребёнка в школу.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Mom is taking the child to school right now.
staged_specs.hint: нести/вести = one trip, carrying/leading; носить/водить = habitual.

staged_specs.title: Choosing motion by transport and context
staged_specs.lesson: Beyond идти/ехать, Russian has separate verb pairs for specific ways of moving — лететь/летать (flying), плыть/плавать (swimming or sailing), бежать/бегать (running) — each following the same one-direction-vs-habitual split.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Птицы летят на юг.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The birds are flying south right now.
staged_specs.hint: Match the verb to how you're moving, then apply the one-direction vs. habitual split.

staged_specs.title: Motion prefixes при-/у-
staged_specs.lesson: Adding при- to a motion verb marks arrival at a destination; adding у- marks departure, often with the sense of leaving for good or being away.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Он пришёл домой поздно, а потом ушёл снова.
staged_specs.exampleEn: He arrived home late, and then left again.
staged_specs.hint: при- = arrive; у- = leave/depart.

staged_specs.title: Motion prefixes в-/вы-
staged_specs.lesson: В- marks entering an enclosed space (with в + accusative), and вы- marks exiting it (with из + genitive).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Она вошла в комнату и вышла из кухни.
staged_specs.exampleEn: She entered the room and exited the kitchen.
staged_specs.hint: в- + в (into); вы- + из (out of).

staged_specs.title: Motion prefixes под-/от-/до-
staged_specs.lesson: Под- marks approaching something (к + dative), от- marks moving away from it (от + genitive), and до- marks reaching a destination or limit (до + genitive).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Автобус подъехал к остановке и доехал до центра.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The bus pulled up to the stop and made it all the way to the center.
staged_specs.hint: под- = approach; от- = move away; до- = reach as far as.

staged_specs.title: Motion prefixes за-/пере-/про-
staged_specs.lesson: За- marks a quick stop along the way or motion behind something, пере- marks crossing from one side to the other, and про- marks passing by or through.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Мы перешли улицу и прошли мимо магазина.
staged_specs.exampleEn: We crossed the street and walked past the store.
staged_specs.hint: за- = drop by / go behind; пере- = cross over; про- = pass by/through.

staged_specs.title: Genitive plural
staged_specs.lesson: Genitive plural endings depend on gender and stem: most masculine nouns add -ов/-ев, most feminine and neuter nouns simply drop their final vowel (with a few exceptions like -ей for soft-stem nouns).
staged_specs.exampleRu: У нас нет свободных мест.
staged_specs.exampleEn: We don't have any free seats.
staged_specs.hint: Masculine usually adds -ов/-ев; feminine/neuter usually drop the ending.

staged_specs.title: Dative plural
staged_specs.lesson: Dative plural is one of the more regular case endings: almost every noun simply takes -ам or -ям (soft stems), regardless of gender.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Учитель дал домашнее задание всем студентам.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The teacher gave homework to all the students.
staged_specs.hint: Dative plural = -ам/-ям, almost always, for every gender.

staged_specs.title: Instrumental plural
staged_specs.lesson: Instrumental plural nouns take -ами or -ями (soft stems), used after instrumental verbs and prepositions like с (with) — the same ending regardless of gender.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я люблю разговаривать с друзьями.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I like talking with my friends.
staged_specs.hint: Instrumental plural = -ами/-ями, same for every gender.

staged_specs.title: Prepositional plural
staged_specs.lesson: Prepositional plural nouns take -ах or -ях (soft stems), used after о (about), в, and на with plural nouns — the same ending regardless of gender.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Мы говорили о новых фильмах.
staged_specs.exampleEn: We were talking about some new movies.
staged_specs.hint: Prepositional plural = -ах/-ях, same for every gender.

staged_specs.title: интересоваться/заниматься + instrumental
staged_specs.lesson: Интересоваться (to be interested in) and заниматься (to be occupied with / study) both govern the instrumental case, not a preposition.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Она интересуется русской литературой.
staged_specs.exampleEn: She's interested in Russian literature.
staged_specs.hint: интересоваться / заниматься + instrumental (no preposition).

staged_specs.title: бояться + genitive
staged_specs.lesson: Бояться (to be afraid of) governs the genitive case directly, with no preposition needed.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Дети боятся тёмной комнаты.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The children are afraid of the dark room.
staged_specs.hint: бояться + genitive (no preposition).

staged_specs.title: помогать + dative
staged_specs.lesson: Помогать (to help) governs the dative case — you help 'to' someone, even though English doesn't use 'to' here.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я помогаю брату с домашним заданием.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I'm helping my brother with his homework.
staged_specs.hint: помогать + dative (the person helped).

staged_specs.title: ждать + genitive or accusative
staged_specs.lesson: Ждать (to wait for) takes the genitive for something abstract or indefinite, but the accusative for a specific, definite person or thing.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я жду автобус, а он ждёт письма.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I'm waiting for the bus, and he's waiting for a letter.
staged_specs.hint: Specific/definite → accusative; abstract/indefinite → genitive.

staged_specs.title: зависеть от + genitive
staged_specs.lesson: Зависеть (to depend) is always followed by от + genitive — 'depend from,' not 'depend on.'
staged_specs.exampleRu: Это зависит от погоды.
staged_specs.exampleEn: It depends on the weather.
staged_specs.hint: зависеть от + genitive.

staged_specs.title: управлять + instrumental
staged_specs.lesson: Управлять (to manage, to drive/operate) governs the instrumental case with no preposition.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Он умеет управлять самолётом.
staged_specs.exampleEn: He knows how to fly a plane.
staged_specs.hint: управлять + instrumental (no preposition).

staged_specs.title: пользоваться + instrumental
staged_specs.lesson: Пользоваться (to use, to make use of) governs the instrumental case with no preposition.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я редко пользуюсь этим словарём.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I rarely use this dictionary.
staged_specs.hint: пользоваться + instrumental (no preposition).

staged_specs.title: благодарить + accusative; благодарен + dative
staged_specs.lesson: The verb благодарить (to thank) takes a direct object in the accusative, but the short-form adjective благодарен (grateful) instead takes the dative for the person being thanked.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я благодарю тебя. Я тебе благодарен.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I thank you. I am grateful to you.
staged_specs.hint: благодарить + accusative; благодарен + dative.

staged_specs.title: Standing, lying, and hanging
staged_specs.lesson: Russian distinguishes HOW an object rests, not just where: стоять (stand, upright objects), лежать (lie, flat objects), and висеть (hang) each pair with the location preposition — English just uses 'is' for all three.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Книга лежит на столе, а лампа стоит рядом.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The book is on the table, and the lamp is standing next to it.
staged_specs.hint: Pick the verb by the object's orientation: стоять (upright) / лежать (flat) / висеть (hanging).

staged_specs.title: Putting, laying, and hanging
staged_specs.lesson: The verbs for PLACING an object mirror its resting position: ставить (stand something up), класть (lay something flat — irregular, not a -ставить verb), and вешать (hang something).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я кладу книгу на стол и вешаю куртку на крючок.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I'm putting the book on the table and hanging my jacket on the hook.
staged_specs.hint: ставить (make it stand) / класть (lay it flat) / вешать (hang it) — match the resulting position.

staged_specs.title: Days and recurrence with в + accusative
staged_specs.lesson: Days of the week use в + accusative to say 'on' that day, and this extends to 'every [day]' with каждый + accusative.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я работаю в понедельник и каждую среду.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I work on Monday and every Wednesday.
staged_specs.hint: в + accusative day = 'on [day]'; каждый + accusative = 'every [day]'.

staged_specs.title: Months and years with в + prepositional
staged_specs.lesson: Months and years use в + prepositional to say 'in' that month or year — a different case than the в + accusative used for days of the week.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я родился в июне, в тысяча девятьсот девяностом году.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I was born in June, in 1990.
staged_specs.hint: в + prepositional = 'in [month/year]' (not accusative, unlike days).

staged_specs.title: Duration: назад and в течение
staged_specs.lesson: Назад (ago) follows a time expression in the accusative and looks back from now; в течение (during, over the course of) takes the genitive and describes a span an action filled.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Два года назад я жил в течение месяца в Москве.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Two years ago, I lived in Moscow for a month.
staged_specs.hint: [time, accusative] + назад = 'ago'; в течение + genitive = 'over the course of'.

staged_specs.title: Deadline and completion: к, за, на
staged_specs.lesson: К + dative marks a deadline ('by' a certain time), за + accusative marks how long a task took to complete, and на + accusative marks how long a result will last.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я закончу работу к пятнице.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I'll finish the work by Friday.
staged_specs.hint: к + dative = deadline 'by'; за + accusative = time taken; на + accusative = duration of result.

staged_specs.title: Productive verb-prefix meanings
staged_specs.lesson: Beyond motion verbs, prefixes systematically add meaning to any verb — по- often means 'a little' or starts an action, за- often means 'begin,' and пере- often means 'redo' or 'too much.'
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я почитал немного, а потом переписал текст заново.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I read a little, and then I rewrote the text from scratch.
staged_specs.hint: по- = a bit/some; за- = begin; пере- = redo/too much.

staged_specs.title: Abstract nouns in -ость
staged_specs.lesson: The suffix -ость turns an adjective into an abstract quality noun, similar to English '-ness': свежий (fresh) → свежесть (freshness).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Его честность всем нравится.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Everyone likes his honesty.
staged_specs.hint: adjective + -ость = the abstract quality (like English '-ness').

staged_specs.title: Event nouns in -ение
staged_specs.lesson: The suffix -ение (or -ание after a vowel) turns a verb into a noun naming the event or process itself, common in formal and written Russian: решить (to decide) → решение (decision).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Правительство приняло важное решение.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The government made an important decision.
staged_specs.hint: verb stem + -ение/-ание = the noun naming that action (formal register).

staged_specs.title: People and roles: -тель/-ник
staged_specs.lesson: -тель and -ник both turn a verb or noun into a person who does or is associated with it: учить (to teach) → учитель (teacher); работа (work) → работник (worker).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Мой сосед — писатель, а его жена — художник.
staged_specs.exampleEn: My neighbor is a writer, and his wife is an artist.
staged_specs.hint: -тель/-ник = the person who does it / is associated with it.

staged_specs.title: Diminutives and stance
staged_specs.lesson: Diminutive suffixes like -ик, -очк-, and -оньк- don't just mean 'small' — they also signal affection, informality, or a softened, warmer tone toward the listener.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Дай мне, пожалуйста, ложечку — маленькую, для ребёнка.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Please give me a little spoon — a small one, for the child.
staged_specs.hint: Diminutives = small AND/OR affectionate, informal tone.

staged_specs.title: Building aspect through prefixation
staged_specs.lesson: Most perfective verbs are built by adding a prefix to an imperfective base — писать (to write) → написать (to finish writing) — but the same prefix can also create a brand-new verb with its own meaning, not just a perfective partner.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я написал письмо, а потом переписал его набело.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I finished writing a letter, and then I recopied it as a clean draft.
staged_specs.hint: Prefix + imperfective can make a perfective partner OR a new verb — check the meaning, not just the form.

staged_specs.title: Specific unknowns with -то
staged_specs.lesson: -то attaches to question words (кто-то, что-то, где-то) to mean a specific but unidentified thing — 'someone/something exists, I just don't know who/what.'
staged_specs.exampleRu: Кто-то звонил тебе, пока тебя не было.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Someone called you while you were out.
staged_specs.hint: -то = a specific unknown ('someone exists, I don't know who').

staged_specs.title: Open-choice unknowns with -нибудь
staged_specs.lesson: -нибудь attaches to question words for an open, any-will-do unknown — common in questions, requests, and future contexts, unlike -то's 'one specific unknown thing.'
staged_specs.exampleRu: Дай мне что-нибудь почитать.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Give me something to read.
staged_specs.hint: -нибудь = any will do (open choice), often in questions/requests.

staged_specs.title: Negative pronouns with ни-
staged_specs.lesson: Ни- pronouns (никто, ничто, никогда) require a doubled negation with не before the verb — unlike English, this isn't a double negative, it's the required Russian pattern.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Никто не звонил мне сегодня.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Nobody called me today.
staged_specs.hint: ни- word + не + verb — both negatives are required, not optional.

staged_specs.title: Genitive under negation
staged_specs.lesson: A direct object often switches from accusative to genitive under negation, especially with abstract nouns or when emphasizing total absence.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я не получил ответа на письмо.
staged_specs.exampleEn: I didn't get an answer to the letter.
staged_specs.hint: Negated verb + object often shifts accusative → genitive (especially for 'none at all').

staged_specs.title: Theme and new information
staged_specs.lesson: Russian word order is driven by information flow, not grammatical role: known/given information (the theme) comes first, and the new, most important information (the rheme) comes last, where it gets the sentence's main stress.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Книгу я купил вчера.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The book, I bought yesterday.
staged_specs.hint: Known info first, new/important info last — word order isn't fixed like in English.

staged_specs.title: Word order for contrastive focus
staged_specs.lesson: Moving a word to the very front of the sentence, out of its normal position, marks it as being contrasted against an alternative — often reinforced with именно (specifically).
staged_specs.exampleRu: Именно Иван, а не Пётр, решил эту проблему.
staged_specs.exampleEn: It was specifically Ivan, not Pyotr, who solved this problem.
staged_specs.hint: Fronting a word (often with именно) marks it as the contrasted, focused item.

staged_specs.title: Forming participles
staged_specs.lesson: Participles are verbal adjectives: active participles (-ущий/-ющий present, -вший past) describe the doer, and passive participles (-емый/-имый present, -нный/-тый past) describe the one acted upon — all agree with their noun like normal adjectives.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Читающий студент не заметил звонок.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The reading student didn't notice the phone call.
staged_specs.hint: Active participle (-ущий/-вший) = the doer; passive (-нный/-емый) = the one acted upon.

staged_specs.title: Reading participial phrases
staged_specs.lesson: A participial phrase is a compressed relative clause: identify the participle, find the noun it's describing (which it agrees with in gender/number/case), then read the rest of the phrase as extra description of that noun.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Студент, читающий книгу, не заметил звонок.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The student reading a book didn't notice the phone call.
staged_specs.hint: Find the participle, find its noun, read the phrase as 'noun who/which [verb]-s'.

staged_specs.title: Participle and который transformations
staged_specs.lesson: Any который-clause (relative clause) can be rewritten as a participial phrase, and vice versa — который agrees with its own noun in gender/number but takes its case from its role inside the clause, while the participle instead agrees fully with the noun it modifies.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Читающий книгу студент не заметил звонок.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The book-reading student didn't notice the phone call.
staged_specs.hint: который + verb ↔ participle — same meaning, different structure.

staged_specs.title: Producing formal participial clauses
staged_specs.lesson: In formal writing, producing your own participial phrases (instead of relying on который) makes prose sound more literary and concise — but requires actively choosing the correct participle type and matching its agreement to the modified noun.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Закон, принятый парламентом вчера, вступит в силу завтра.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The law, passed by parliament yesterday, will take effect tomorrow.
staged_specs.hint: Choose active vs. passive, present vs. past, then agree it fully with the noun it modifies.

staged_specs.title: Simultaneous verbal adverbs
staged_specs.lesson: Imperfective verbal adverbs (gerunds) ending in -я/-а describe an action happening AT THE SAME TIME as the main verb, done by the same subject.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Читая книгу, она пила чай.
staged_specs.exampleEn: While reading a book, she drank tea.
staged_specs.hint: Imperfective gerund (-я/-а) = happening at the same time as the main verb.

staged_specs.title: Prior-action verbal adverbs
staged_specs.lesson: Perfective verbal adverbs (gerunds) ending in -в/-вши describe an action completed BEFORE the main verb, done by the same subject.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Прочитав книгу, она пошла спать.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Having finished the book, she went to sleep.
staged_specs.hint: Perfective gerund (-в/-вши) = completed before the main verb happens.

staged_specs.title: Concession with хотя
staged_specs.lesson: Хотя (although) introduces a fact that would seem to contradict the main clause, without denying either part — both things are simply true at once.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Хотя было холодно, мы пошли гулять.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Although it was cold, we went for a walk.
staged_specs.hint: хотя + [surprising fact], [main clause anyway] — both parts stay true.

staged_specs.title: Concession with несмотря на
staged_specs.lesson: Несмотря на (despite, in spite of) takes an accusative noun phrase rather than a full clause — a more compact, formal alternative to хотя for the same concessive meaning.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Несмотря на дождь, мы пошли гулять.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.
staged_specs.hint: несмотря на + accusative noun phrase (not a full clause, unlike хотя).

staged_specs.title: Formal connective contrasts
staged_specs.lesson: Formal/written Russian favors тем не менее (nevertheless) and однако (however) over the conversational но, especially at the start of a sentence, to signal a more measured, written-register contrast.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Прогноз был плохим; тем не менее, мы выиграли.
staged_specs.exampleEn: The forecast was bad; nevertheless, we won.
staged_specs.hint: тем не менее / однако = formal-register 'but' (written, more measured than но).

staged_specs.title: Discourse particle же
staged_specs.lesson: Же adds emphasis or contrast to the word right before it, often translating as 'though,' 'after all,' or just added stress — it never changes the sentence's grammar, only its emphasis.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Я же говорил тебе об этом!
staged_specs.exampleEn: I did tell you about that!
staged_specs.hint: же emphasizes/contrasts the word before it — no grammar change, just stress.

staged_specs.title: Discourse particle ведь
staged_specs.lesson: Ведь introduces a justification or reminder the listener should already know or accept — roughly 'after all' or 'you know' — softening a statement into a shared, obvious truth.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Не волнуйся, ведь у нас есть время.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Don't worry, we have time after all.
staged_specs.hint: ведь = 'after all/you know' — frames the point as an obvious, shared reason.

staged_specs.title: Contrastive particle -то
staged_specs.lesson: As a contrastive particle (distinct from the indefinite -то in кто-то), -то attached directly to a word singles it out against an implied alternative — 'that one at least, even if nothing else.'
staged_specs.exampleRu: Работать-то я работаю, но денег всё равно мало.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Working, sure I'm working, but there's still not much money.
staged_specs.hint: Contrastive -то singles out a word: 'that much is true, at least.'

staged_specs.title: Stance particle уж
staged_specs.lesson: Уж intensifies a statement with a note of resignation, certainty, or mild exasperation — often paired with a stressed word to mean 'really' or 'for sure,' colored by the speaker's attitude.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Уж я-то знаю, как это трудно.
staged_specs.exampleEn: If anyone knows how hard this is, it's certainly me.
staged_specs.hint: уж = intensifies with resignation/certainty — adds the speaker's attitude, not new facts.

staged_specs.title: News-report register
staged_specs.lesson: News reports favor passive constructions, nominalized verbs (-ение/-ание nouns), and impersonal phrasing over the direct, personal statements of everyday speech.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Сегодня было объявлено о повышении цен.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Today, a price increase was announced.
staged_specs.hint: News register: passive voice + nominalized verbs (-ение), avoiding a stated 'who.'

staged_specs.title: Official-statement register
staged_specs.lesson: Official/bureaucratic Russian relies on set formulaic phrases (в соответствии с — in accordance with) and long chains of genitive nouns instead of everyday verbs and clauses.
staged_specs.exampleRu: В соответствии с решением комиссии, заявление было отклонено.
staged_specs.exampleEn: In accordance with the commission's decision, the application was rejected.
staged_specs.hint: Official register: fixed formulas + genitive noun chains, not everyday verbs.

staged_specs.title: Academic hedging and argumentation
staged_specs.lesson: Academic Russian hedges claims with phrases like по-видимому (apparently) and builds arguments with explicit connectives (следовательно — therefore) rather than stating conclusions bluntly.
staged_specs.exampleRu: Следовательно, данная гипотеза представляется наиболее вероятной.
staged_specs.exampleEn: Therefore, this hypothesis appears to be the most likely.
staged_specs.hint: Academic register: hedge with по-видимому/представляется + explicit connectives (следовательно).
